title: TM4C123 Simulator — real firmware on a simulated LaunchPad

scenes.title: The LaunchPad workspace
scenes.caption: This is the TM4C123 Simulator: TI's EK-TM4C123GXL LaunchPad, placed from TI's CAD data, in an interactive circuit workspace.

scenes.title: Real C source
scenes.caption: The firmware is plain C written against the TM4C123 registers: three hardware timers, each with its own interrupt handler.

scenes.title: GCC compilation
scenes.caption: Compile runs the real arm-none-eabi-gcc toolchain. The inspector shows the resulting Cortex-M4 ELF and its sections.

scenes.title: ELF execution in Renode, RGB LED
scenes.caption: Run loads that ELF into Renode, which executes it on an emulated Cortex-M4 with the project's TM4C123 peripheral models. Three timer interrupts toggle the RGB LED; every pin change is a simulator event.

scenes.title: Interactive wiring
scenes.caption: Circuits are built by dragging from a header pin to a part; the wire is checked and routed clear of the other pins.

scenes.title: External button
scenes.caption: Here the firmware polls an external pushbutton on PA6. Hold it: the pin reads low, and the firmware drives PA7 high to light the external LED.

scenes.title: LCD1602 driven by firmware
scenes.caption: An LCD1602 in 4-bit mode. The display shows only what the firmware's GPIO writes tell the HD44780 model: a greeting, a custom CGRAM heart, and a counter.

scenes.title: ADC potentiometer
scenes.caption: A potentiometer feeds ADC0 on PE3. Turn the knob: the pin table shows the voltage, and the firmware's 12-bit reading switches the LED from green to red.

scenes.title: Compiler diagnostics
scenes.caption: Mistakes are reported as GCC reports them. The Problems list shows the error with GCC's own suggestion and jumps to its line. The fix rebuilds cleanly.

scenes.title: Console and limits
scenes.caption: The console groups every simulator message by severity and source. This runs locally in trusted mode; timing is approximate and not yet validated against physical hardware.
